analysis.one_liner: Restores overtime pay protections taken away by a 2004 Labor Department rule and keeps the salary cutoff rising with wages.
analysis.headline: The bill, backed by a bipartisan group of 16 senators, never got past a Senate committee and died when the 109th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: In 2004, the Labor Department rewrote the rules deciding which workers count as salaried 'executives' and therefore lose the right to overtime pay. This bill would cancel every part of that rule that removed overtime rights from anyone who had them under the older rules, restoring the protections in place as of March 2003. It would also raise the salary threshold below which workers automatically qualify for overtime — from a 1975 level of $155 a week to $591 a week — and automatically increase it every year with executive pay, so inflation could not quietly erode overtime protections again.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers whose jobs were reclassified out of overtime protection by the 2004 rule — often salaried employees making modest wages who were labeled executive, administrative, or professional and thereby lost the right to time-and-a-half pay for hours over 40. Millions of such workers would regain or keep the right to overtime, and the indexed salary threshold would protect low- and middle-income salaried workers going forward.

how_it_helps.text: It strikes down every portion of the April 23, 2004 Labor Department rule that exempts from overtime any employee who would not have been exempt under the regulations in effect on March 31, 2003, and reinstates those older protections [S2] [S3].

It raises the minimum salary level for the executive, administrative, and managerial overtime exemption from the 1975 baseline of $155 per week to $591 per week, an amount tied to growth in the Employment Cost Index for those occupations [S3].

It requires the Secretary of Labor to increase the salary threshold every December 31 by the annual rise in the Employment Cost Index, preventing future inflation from quietly shrinking overtime coverage [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Employers who currently pay salaries to workers exempted under the 2004 rule would owe time-and-a-half for overtime hours for many of them, raising labor costs in retail, restaurants, insurance, and other salaried workplaces.

drawbacks.text: Restoring overtime eligibility raises labor costs for employers, which some would meet by cutting base salaries, capping hours, or shifting workers to hourly schedules, so not every affected worker would end up with more money [S3].

The bill works by statutorily nullifying a specific regulation and overriding administrative review procedures, an intrusive way to settle a rulemaking dispute that business groups argued made Labor Department rules harder to update by any method [S2] [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For workers classified as exempt under the 2004 rule, restored overtime rights were worth real money — the whole point of the bill was to undo a specific loss. The cost falls on employers as higher payroll costs, and some workers could see hours capped or pay restructured in response. The indexed threshold is a sensible fix to a known problem: the old $155-a-week cutoff had been left unchanged for decades so that inflation shrank overtime coverage year after year.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate labor committee the day it was introduced, the committee never took it up, and it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Harkin introduced the bill on January 31, 2005, joined by 13 Democratic colleagues and one Republican, Arlen Specter [S3] [S4].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee on the day of introduction; no further action was ever recorded [S1] [S5].
The bill received no committee markup, no floor vote, and no House action before the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007 [S1] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers who benefited from the 2004 overtime rule kept the narrower overtime protections, since the rule was never rolled back. The Labor Department's 2004 rules stayed in effect for the rest of the Congress.

for.name: Sen. Tom Harkin
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Overtime Rights Protection Act and delivered introductory remarks on the Senate floor [S3] [S5].

for.name: 14 of 44 Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including Kennedy, Kerry, Levin, Murray, Stabenow, Mikulski, Dodd, Leahy, Rockefeller, and Sarbanes [S3] [S4].

for.name: Sen. Arlen Specter
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it a bipartisan pair at introduction [S3] [S4].

against.name: Senate HELP Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Sen. Mike Enzi (R-WY)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral and never scheduled a markup or vote; no action after the January 31, 2005 referral appears in the record [S1] [S5].

against.name: Bush administration Labor Department
against.role: Author of the April 2004 overtime rule the bill would repeal
against.what_they_did: Had issued the 2004 rule revising overtime exemptions that the bill sought to nullify; the administration opposed rolling it back.

sides.party_line_note: All 14 Democratic cosponsors signed on, but only 1 of the Senate's 55 Republicans (Specter) joined, and with Republicans holding the Senate majority and the committee chair, the bill went nowhere.

industries.industry: Employers of salaried workers (retail, restaurants, insurance, banking, and other exempt-heavy industries)
industries.note: The bill would have re-imposed time-and-a-half overtime pay on many workers the 2004 rule had reclassified as exempt, raising payroll costs. Its interest in the bill ran against the workers it currently pays flat salaries for long hours.

industries.industry: Hourly and salaried workers near the overtime cutoff
industries.note: Workers whose overtime rights were stripped by the 2004 rule, and low-paid salaried workers near the threshold, would gain the right to overtime or higher pay for extra hours.
